---
title: "Build your own color picker"
---

![The finished color picker: the top half previews colors while the mouse moves, the bottom half keeps the color chosen with the last click, and the corner lists its HSB values.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0020-Variables/color_picker.png){width=360}

In the chapter about mixing colors you used an online color picker: point
at a color, read off its numbers. By now you know enough to build one
yourself. The project brings together almost everything from this part:
mouse events, the HSB color model, the system variables `width` and
`height`, constants with explicit types, and text output with a template
string. And it hides a small surprise: the program remembers your chosen
color without a single variable of your own.

## Two halves, two jobs {#sec-picker-halves}

The picker splits its canvas into two halves with different jobs. The
**top half** is the preview: it changes its color on every mouse movement.
Moving the mouse to the right walks the hue along the rainbow, moving it
down increases the saturation. The **bottom half** is the result: when the
user clicks, it takes on the current color and keeps it until the next
click. Next to it, in the lower left corner, the program writes the HSB
values of the chosen color, so the user can copy them into another
program.

![The layout of the color picker: horizontal movement controls the hue, vertical movement the saturation, and the canvas measures 360 by 200 pixels.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0020-Variables/color_picker_mouse.png){width=420}

## A canvas size with a purpose {#sec-picker-canvas-size}

Look at the measurements in the layout picture. The canvas is 360 pixels
wide, and the hue scale runs from 0 to 360. The top half is 100 pixels
tall, and saturation runs from 0 to 100. That is no coincidence, it's the
whole trick of this program: the mouse position doesn't have to be
converted at all, it *is* the color. `mouseX` is the hue, `mouseY` is the
saturation, and the brightness simply stays at 100:

```typescript
function mouseMoved() {
  fill(mouseX, mouseY, 100);
  rect(0, 0, width, height / 2);
}
```

The `rect` statement covers exactly the top half: its corner is (0, 0),
its width is the canvas width, and its height is half the canvas height.
Notice what is *not* here: no `background` call. The rectangle repaints
the whole preview by itself, and the bottom half must not be erased
anyway, because it holds the chosen color.

## A second mouse event: `mouseClicked` {#sec-mouse-clicked}

The mouse can do more than move. When you press and release a mouse
button, that's a **click**, and p5.js treats it as an event of its own.
Write a function called `mouseClicked`, and p5.js calls it automatically
once per click:

```typescript
function mouseClicked() {
  // runs once for every click
}
```

Everything you know about `mouseMoved` applies here too: the name is an
agreement between you and p5.js, so a typo like `mouseclicked` gives you a
function that is never called, without any error message. Inside
`mouseClicked`, the system variables `mouseX` and `mouseY` hold the
position where the click happened.

## Freezing the chosen color {#sec-picker-freeze}

When the click arrives, the program reads the color from the mouse
position and stores the two interesting values in constants:

```typescript
const colorHue: number = mouseX;
const colorSaturation: number = min(100, mouseY);
```

The second line needs a moment of thought. The user may click anywhere on
the canvas, including the bottom half, and there `mouseY` runs up to 200.
A saturation of 200 doesn't exist; the scale ends at 100. The function
`min` from the responsive robot chapter solves that: `min(a, b)` returns
the smaller of the two values, so `min(100, mouseY)` caps the saturation
at 100. In the top half, where `mouseY` is at most 100, `min` changes
nothing. Used like this, `min` is a guard: it keeps a value inside its
allowed range.

With the two constants in hand, the rest of `mouseClicked` is drawing you
know: set `fill(colorHue, colorSaturation, 100)`, cover the bottom half
with a `rect`, then switch the fill to black and write the values with a
template string:

```typescript
text(`H: ${colorHue}, S: ${colorSaturation}, B: 100`, 5, height - 5);
```

Mind the order: the text must be drawn *after* the rectangle, or the
freshly painted bottom half covers it up.

## A program that remembers without a variable {#sec-picker-paint-remembers}

One thing about the color picker is worth noticing before you build it.
The program remembers the chosen color between events, across hundreds of
`mouseMoved` calls, and yet it declares no global variable. The memory is
the paint itself: nothing ever repaints the bottom half except the next
click, so the color simply stays on the canvas. That works here because
the program only has to remember one single thing, and that thing is
literally a color. In the next chapter, a program has to remember a
growing list of values, and there paint alone won't be enough.

## Your exercise: Color picker {#sec-color-picker-exercise}

Build the picker in this order:

1. **Set the stage in `setup`.** Create the 360 by 200 canvas, switch to
   HSB with `colorMode(HSB)`, and add `noStroke()` so the rectangles have
   no outlines. Paint the whole canvas with a starting color; the sample
   uses `background(0, 100, 100)`, a fully saturated red.
2. **Fill `mouseMoved`.** Set the fill color from the mouse position and
   cover the top half with a rectangle.
3. **Fill `mouseClicked`.** Declare the two constants with explicit data
   types, including the `min` guard, paint the bottom half in the chosen
   color, and write the HSB values in black in the lower left corner. The
   text is a format promise: `H: 208, S: 92, B: 100`, with exactly these
   letters, colons, and commas.
4. **Test the tool.** Move the mouse along the top edge and watch the
   preview walk through the rainbow, then move it downward and watch the
   colors fade toward white. Click in the top half and check the bottom
   half and the text. Finally, click deep in the bottom half: the
   saturation in the text must never climb above 100, because the `min`
   guard caps it.
